claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory calculations can be used to test for a ferromagnetic ground state.
A ferromagnetic ground state can be assessed by comparing the total energies of ferromagnetic spin-polarized, non-spin-polarized, and antiferromagnetic configurations.
A calculation without spin polarization represents a non-magnetic or paramagnetic configuration.
The proposed calculations are performed at zero temperature.
The proposed calculations use periodic boundary conditions on a crystalline unit cell.
Electronic exchange is especially significant in materials containing transition-metal atoms.
Crystal structure and atomic positions determine exchange pathways between magnetic ions.
Exchange interactions among localized or itinerant electrons can favor parallel spin alignment.
If ferromagnetism is present, parallel spin alignment lowers the calculated total energy.
A ferromagnetic solution should have a lower total energy than the non-spin-polarized or antiferromagnetic solutions.
A lower-energy spin-polarized solution with a net magnetic moment indicates ferromagnetic ordering.
Non-spin-polarized or antiferromagnetic calculations do not account for ferromagnetic exchange effects.
The choice of exchange-correlation functional can affect quantitative magnetic predictions from DFT.
Zero-temperature DFT has limitations in predicting temperature-dependent magnetic behavior.
Predicted energy differences and magnetic moments may vary with computational parameters.
Further corrections may be needed to represent finite-temperature magnetic behavior accurately.
Failure to obtain both a lower total energy and a significant net magnetic moment in the spin-polarized calculation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats an antiferromagnetic spin-polarized calculation as a valid energetic comparator, while the baseline groups it with non-spin-polarized calculations and says it does not account for ferromagnetic exchange effects. An antiferromagnetic DFT configuration can include spin polarization and exchange interactions even though its ordering is not ferromagnetic.
